Validate the following vignette.

Patient demographics:
  age: 27
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: Middle Eastern
  relationship_status: Married
  occupation: Physical Therapist
  trauma_type: Sexual assault
  pcl5: 49

Patient-reported symptoms:
  Triggers: Olfactory (Cologne/Perfume): A specific perfume or cologne, Somatic (Pain): Physical pain in a part of the body, Sexual Situations: Sexual situations or intimacy
  Maladaptive Strategies: Dissociation: I pretend it happened to someone else, Avoid Thinking: Thinking about the event, Body Monitoring: constantly check body for signs of danger or injury
  Threat: Startle Response: Feeling jumpy or easily startled, Startle to Touch: I react with alarm when someone touches me unexpectedly, Startle to Movement: Unexpected movement nearby causes me to react as if I am in danger
  Negative Appraisals: Lost Emotions: I will never be able to feel normal emotions again, Can't Rely on Self: I can't rely on myself, Body Shame: I feel ashamed of what happened to my body

Vignette:
Yusuf, a 27-year-old physical therapist of Middle Eastern descent, had always taken pride in his ability to help others heal. He had a warm demeanor, a comforting presence that eased his patients’ anxieties. Yet, beneath this exterior lay an overwhelming burden that had increasingly stifled his joy and purpose. It all began with a traumatic event that shattered his sense of safety and self. 

One evening after a social gathering, Yusuf was assaulted by someone he had considered a friend. The details were hazy, overshadowed by a thick cloud of disbelief and shame. It wasn’t just the physical violation that haunted him; it was the profound violation of trust that gnawed at his psyche. In the weeks that followed, he found himself replaying the event in his mind, desperately trying to reconcile the person he had been with the person he now felt compelled to become.

As the days turned into weeks, Yusuf noticed that certain scents had become unbearable. He could no longer walk into his favorite café without being assaulted by the smell of a cologne that reminded him of that night. It would hit him like a wave, sending him spiraling back into the moment of terror, where he felt trapped and powerless. Each time he caught a whiff, his heart raced, and he felt a cold sweat break out across his skin. The world around him would blur, and he would retreat into himself, pretending it had happened to someone else, as if distancing himself from the pain could somehow lessen it.

His body became a battleground. Over time, Yusuf developed an intense awareness of every ache and pain, constantly monitoring himself for signs of danger. The assault had left him feeling vulnerable, as if his body no longer belonged to him. He began to associate any physical discomfort with the trauma, convinced that he was somehow still in danger. It was as if the very essence of his being had turned against him, and with every twinge or cramp, he was reminded of his own fragility.

In the context of his work, Yusuf's symptoms became increasingly problematic. His close interactions with patients often involved physical touch—something he had always enjoyed before the assault. Now, he flinched at the slightest unexpected touch, jumping as if he were under siege. His colleagues noticed his heightened startle response and the way he seemed withdrawn, but he brushed off their concerns, convincing himself that he was just having a rough time adjusting. He had come to believe that he could not rely on himself, that he was somehow broken and would never return to the person he had once been.

As intimacy with his wife became fraught with anxiety, Yusuf withdrew further into himself. He felt ashamed of his body and the memories it carried. The thought of sexual situations sent him spiraling into panic, and he found himself avoiding closeness altogether. He loved his wife deeply but felt he was doing her a disservice by not being able to engage fully in their relationship. He feared that his inability to navigate intimacy would push her away, leaving him even more isolated in his pain. 

It was during a particularly difficult evening, fraught with tension and unspoken words, that Yusuf finally broke down. He had been quiet and distant, lost in a whirlpool of shame and self-loathing, when he felt the familiar pang of sadness wash over him. His wife, noticing his distress, held him close, whispering words of comfort. In that moment, Yusuf realized he couldn’t continue living like this. The thought of never being able to feel normal emotions again loomed over him like a dark cloud.

Seeking help became his last hope. He recognized that he could no longer pretend that everything was okay or that he could handle this alone. As he walked into the therapist’s office for the first time, he felt a mixture of hope and fear. He feared what he might have to confront, but more than that, he hoped to reclaim his life—the joy he once had, the intimacy he longed for, and the trust he had lost in himself. Yusuf knew the journey ahead would be challenging, but he yearned to heal, to reconnect with the man he used to be, and to embrace his life once more.
